title: Roots of unity and common orders
promptMarkdown:
1. Let $G$ be a group and $a\in G$ with $a^m=e$ and $a^n=e$ for positive integers $m,n$. Prove that $a^{\gcd(m,n)}=e$. Deduce that if $a$ has finite order $k$ then $a^j=e$ if and only if $k\mid j$.
2. For $n\ge1$ let $\mu_n=\{z\in\mathbb C: z^n=1\}$. Prove that $\mu_m\cap\mu_n=\mu_{\gcd(m,n)}$, and determine $\mu_{12}\cap\mu_8$ explicitly as a set of complex numbers.
3. Let $\omega=\operatorname{cis}(2\pi/n)$. Prove that $\omega^k$ is a primitive $n$th root of unity (that is, generates $\mu_n$) if and only if $\gcd(k,n)=1$, and list the primitive $12$th roots of unity as powers of $\omega$.
hintLadder: Bézout: $\gcd(m,n)=mr+ns$ for some integers $r,s$, possibly negative. Raise $a$ to that power using the exponent laws.
For the deduction, apply part 1 to $j$ and $k$ and compare $\gcd(j,k)$ with the minimality of $k$.
An element of $\mu_m\cap\mu_n$ satisfies two equations at once; part 1 applies in the group $\mathbb C^*$. For the reverse inclusion, $\gcd(m,n)$ divides both $m$ and $n$.
$|\omega^k|=n/\gcd(k,n)$ by Theorem 4.1.13; when does this equal $n$? Which $k\in\{1,\dots,12\}$ are coprime to $12$?

deterministicChecks.description: gcd(m, n) appears in the argument (Bézout or the intersection formula)
μ_12 ∩ μ_8 is identified as μ_4 = {1, i, −1, −i}

criteria.criterion: a^{gcd(m,n)} = (a^m)^r (a^n)^s = e via Bézout; then a^j = e ⇒ a^{gcd(j,k)} = e with 0 < gcd(j,k) ≤ k forces gcd(j,k) = k, i.e. k | j, and the converse is immediate.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Bézout used correctly (negative exponents allowed) and the divisibility deduced from minimality.

levels.label: not met
levels.description: Missing, or argues with mn instead of the gcd.

criteria.criterion: Both inclusions: μ_{gcd} ⊂ μ_m ∩ μ_n because gcd divides m and n; μ_m ∩ μ_n ⊂ μ_{gcd} by part 1 in C*.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: μ_4 named without the elements, or one element wrong.

criteria.criterion: ω^k generates μ_n iff its order n/gcd(k,n) equals n iff gcd(k,n) = 1 (using that μ_n = ⟨ω⟩ has order n); the primitive 12th roots are ω, ω^5, ω^7, ω^11.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Argument via the order formula and the correct list of four.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: List right, argument incomplete, or argument right with a slip in the list.

checkExamples.label: LaTeX argument
checkExamples.text: By Bézout write gcd(m,n) = mr + ns with $r,s\in\mathbb Z$, so $a^{\gcd(m,n)}=(a^m)^r(a^n)^s=e$. Applying this in $\mathbb C^*$, $\mu_{12}\cap\mu_8=\mu_{\gcd(12,8)}=\mu_4=\{1,i,-1,-i\}$.

checkExamples.label: plain-text fourth roots
checkExamples.text: gcd(12,8) = 4, so the common solutions are the fourth roots of unity: 1, i, -1 and -i.

checkExamples.label: lcm confusion
checkExamples.text: μ_12 ∩ μ_8 = μ_24, the 24th roots of unity, since lcm(12,8) = 24.

checkExamples.label: product instead of gcd
checkExamples.text: Since a^m = e and a^n = e we have a^{mn} = e, so the order of a divides mn.
